## Solution

We consider the homogeneous Fredholm integral equation with symmetric kernel $K(x,t)=xt$ on $[0,1]$:

$$\int_0^1 K(x,t)\,\varphi(t)\,dt = \lambda\,\varphi(x). \tag{1}$$

Since $K(x,t)=xt$ is symmetric, its eigenvalues are real, and the Ritz (Rayleigh–Ritz) method applies: we restrict the Rayleigh quotient

$$\lambda[\varphi]=\frac{\displaystyle\iint_0^1 K(x,t)\,\varphi(x)\,\varphi(t)\,dx\,dt}{\displaystyle\int_0^1 \varphi(x)^2\,dx} \tag{2}$$

to a finite-dimensional trial subspace and find its stationary values.

### One-term approximation

Take the single coordinate function $u_1(x)=x$, which is the natural candidate (it is the "shape" of the kernel in the $x$-direction). Set $\varphi(x)=c_1 x$. Then

$$\iint_0^1 xt\,(c_1 x)(c_1 t)\,dx\,dt = c_1^2\!\left(\int_0^1 x^2\,dx\right)\!\left(\int_0^1 t^2\,dt\right)=c_1^2\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac13=\frac{c_1^2}{9},$$

$$\int_0^1 (c_1 x)^2\,dx = c_1^2\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{c_1^2}{3}.$$

The Rayleigh quotient gives

$$\lambda_1 \approx \frac{c_1^2/9}{c_1^2/3} = \frac{1}{3}. \tag{3}$$

### Two-term verification

To confirm this is the smallest (positive) eigenvalue, enlarge the subspace with $u_1(x)=x$, $u_2(x)=x^2$, and set $\varphi=c_1 u_1+c_2 u_2$. The Ritz equations $\sum_j a_{ij}c_j=\lambda\sum_j b_{ij}c_j$ use

$$a_{ij}=\iint xt\,u_i(x)u_j(t)\,dx\,dt,\qquad b_{ij}=\int_0^1 u_i(x)u_j(x)\,dx.$$

Computing:

$$a_{11}=\tfrac19,\quad a_{12}=\tfrac1{12},\quad a_{22}=\tfrac1{16},\qquad b_{11}=\tfrac13,\quad b_{12}=\tfrac14,\quad b_{22}=\tfrac15.$$

The characteristic equation is

$$\det\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac19-\tfrac{\lambda}{3} & \tfrac1{12}-\tfrac{\lambda}{4}\\[2pt] \tfrac1{12}-\tfrac{\lambda}{4} & \tfrac1{16}-\tfrac{\lambda}{5}\end{pmatrix}=0.$$

Expanding the determinant:

$$\left(\tfrac19-\tfrac{\lambda}{3}\right)\!\left(\tfrac1{16}-\tfrac{\lambda}{5}\right)-\left(\tfrac1{12}-\tfrac{\lambda}{4}\right)^2=0.$$

After simplification the constant terms cancel ($\tfrac1{144}-\tfrac1{144}=0$), leaving

$$\lambda^2\!\left(\tfrac1{15}-\tfrac1{16}\right)+\lambda\!\left(-\tfrac1{45}-\tfrac1{48}+\tfrac1{24}\right)=\frac{\lambda^2}{240}-\frac{\lambda}{720}=0,$$

so

$$\lambda\left(\frac{\lambda}{240}-\frac{1}{720}\right)=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \lambda=0\;\text{or}\;\lambda=\frac{240}{720}=\frac13.$$

The root $\lambda=0$ corresponds to the trivial (infinite-multiplicity) null eigenvalue of the rank-one kernel; the **smallest positive eigenvalue** is

$$\boxed{\lambda_{\min}\approx \dfrac{1}{3}\approx 0.3333}.$$

### Remark (exactness)

The kernel $K(x,t)=xt$ is separable (rank one), so it has exactly one nonzero eigenvalue. Substituting $\varphi(x)=x$ into (1):

$$\int_0^1 xt\cdot t\,dt = x\int_0^1 t^2\,dt = \frac{x}{3} = \frac13\,\varphi(x),$$

confirming $\lambda=1/3$ is the exact nonzero eigenvalue. The Ritz approximation with the trial function $u_1(x)=x$ therefore recovers the exact value, and the two-term computation shows no smaller positive eigenvalue exists.

### PROOF COMPLETE
